questions.stem:
A 24-year-old woman develops vigorous vomiting and cramping 2 hours after eating fried rice from a restaurant. The kitchen cooks a large batch of rice in the morning, keeps it at room temperature, and stir-fries portions to order in the evening. She has no fever and feels well by the next morning.

Which of the following best describes the organism responsible?
choices: Gram-negative rod producing Shiga-like toxin
Gram-negative curved rod that grows best at 42 C
Gram-positive coccus in clusters from a food handler's skin
Anaerobic gram-positive rod whose toxin blocks acetylcholine release
Gram-positive spore-forming rod with a heat-stable emetic toxin

explain.html:
Vomiting 1 to 6 hours after eating rice that was cooked, held, then briefly stir-fried is the emetic syndrome of Bacillus cereus, a gram-positive, spore-forming rod common in the environment and on grains.

The spores survive the first cooking. If the rice is held without refrigeration, they germinate into bacteria that make the heat-stable emetic toxin, and stir-frying does not destroy it. B. cereus also has a diarrheal form, 8 to 16 hours after viable spores are eaten and make toxin in the intestine.
why: Shiga-like toxin describes EHEC, which causes bloody diarrhea days later.
A curved rod that grows at 42 C is Campylobacter, which causes later-onset diarrhea.
Staph aureus causes a similar syndrome, but the fried-rice holding story points to B. cereus.
Neurotoxin blocking acetylcholine release describes Clostridium botulinum.
explain.takeaway: Bacillus cereus spores survive cooking of rice; held rice develops a heat-stable emetic toxin that causes vomiting 1 to 6 hours after eating.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
At a hospital cafeteria, 40 employees develop crampy abdominal pain and watery diarrhea without vomiting or fever between 8 and 16 hours after a lunch of roast beef with gravy. The roast and gravy had been cooked the day before in a large batch and cooled slowly at room temperature before reheating. Symptoms resolve within a day.

Which of the following organisms is most likely responsible?
choices: Staphylococcus aureus
Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi
Clostridium perfringens
Vibrio cholerae
Listeria monocytogenes

explain.html:
Watery diarrhea 8 to 16 hours after a large-batch meat and gravy meal served at a cafeteria, prison or banquet is the signature of Clostridium perfringens, a spore-forming gram-positive rod. Spores survive cooking and germinate in slowly cooled meats and gravies, and the ingested enterotoxin causes diarrhea.

The incubation is longer than Staph aureus (3 to 4 hours, vomiting), and the illness is brief and afebrile, unlike invasive pathogens. A distinct type C toxin causes the severe, possibly bloody syndrome called pigbel.
why: Staph aureus causes vomiting within 3 to 4 hours, not diarrhea at 8 to 16 hours.
Typhoid has a 5 to 21 day incubation with fever.
Cholera comes from contaminated water and causes massive watery diarrhea.
Listeria is linked to deli meats and cheese, with invasive disease in high-risk hosts.
explain.takeaway: Clostridium perfringens causes afebrile watery diarrhea 8 to 16 hours after large-batch meats and gravies cooled slowly.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 34-year-old restaurant cook develops fever, cramps and diarrhea 2 days after eating undercooked eggs at home. Stool culture grows Salmonella enteritidis. He is otherwise healthy, recovers in 4 days with fluids, and asks to return to work.

Which of the following is the most appropriate advice?
choices: Return to work now, since symptoms have resolved
Take ciprofloxacin to shorten carriage, then return
Return once a stool culture is negative
Return after 1 dose of the oral typhoid vaccine
Return after 12 months of negative cultures

explain.html:
Nontyphoidal Salmonella gastroenteritis in a healthy adult is managed supportively. Antibiotics are usually not necessary for GI illness except in the very young, the very old and the immunocompromised, and they may lengthen the period of carriage, which matters most for food handlers and health care workers.

For that reason, food handlers and health care workers cannot return to work until a stool culture is negative. Prevention otherwise relies on proper food preparation and storage.
why: Resolution of symptoms does not mean he has stopped shedding the organism.
Antibiotics may prolong carriage, not shorten it, in uncomplicated Salmonella.
The typhoid vaccine does not clear an existing nontyphoidal Salmonella infection.
Twelve months of positive cultures defines chronic typhoid carriage, not a return-to-work rule.
explain.takeaway: In uncomplicated nontyphoidal Salmonella, antibiotics may prolong carriage, and food handlers and health care workers return only after a negative stool culture.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 27-year-old man returns from 4 weeks visiting relatives in rural South Asia. Over the last 10 days he has had gradually rising fever, headache and abdominal pain with constipation. Temperature is 39.8 C (103.6 F) and pulse is 74/min. He has a few faint pink macules on the abdomen and the spleen is palpable. Stool culture is negative.

Which of the following is the most appropriate test to confirm the diagnosis?
choices: Repeat stool culture on a selective medium
Modified acid-fast stain of stool
Stool assay for Shiga toxin
Serum IgM for hepatitis A
Blood cultures

explain.html:
A gradually climbing fever with relative bradycardia, abdominal pain, rose spots and splenomegaly after travel to an area with poor sanitation is typhoid fever, caused by Salmonella typhi, a human-only pathogen with a 5 to 21 day incubation. By the third week it can cause intestinal bleeding, perforation and sepsis.

Typhoid is diagnosed by blood cultures. Unlike nontyphoidal Salmonella, it is treated with antibiotics (ceftriaxone, with susceptibility checks in travelers), and a vaccine is available.
why: Stool culture is the test for Salmonella enterocolitis; typhoid is a bloodstream illness.
Modified acid-fast stain detects Cryptosporidium and Cyclospora.
Shiga toxin assays are for EHEC.
Hepatitis A causes jaundice and very high liver enzymes, not rose spots.
explain.takeaway: Typhoid fever (S. typhi: rising fever, relative bradycardia, rose spots) is diagnosed by blood cultures and treated with antibiotics such as ceftriaxone.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
Several toddlers and two staff members at a daycare center develop fever, cramping abdominal pain, tenesmus and frequent small-volume stools with blood and mucus. There was no common food or animal exposure. The outbreak spread rapidly even though staff report that only minor lapses in diaper-changing hygiene occurred. Stool culture grows a non-lactose-fermenting gram-negative rod.

Which feature of this organism best explains how easily it spread?
choices: Spores that resist hand sanitizer
Large reservoir in poultry and wild birds that contaminates food
Very low infectious dose with a human reservoir
Growth at refrigerator temperatures
Preformed toxin in shared food

explain.html:
Dysentery (fever, tenesmus, bloody mucoid stools) spreading person to person in a daycare is classic Shigella sonnei. Humans are the usual reservoir, and spread is by direct or indirect contact with feces, or through food or water contaminated by a food handler.

Its infectious dose is very low (about 10 organisms), so small lapses in hygiene are enough. The bacteria invade the bowel wall, causing more severe illness than many food-associated pathogens. Shiga toxin was first isolated from Shigella. Diagnosis is by stool culture.
why: Shigella is not a spore former.
Poultry and wild birds are reservoirs for Campylobacter and Salmonella.
Cold tolerance describes Listeria.
No shared food was involved, and Shigella invades rather than acting through preformed toxin.
explain.takeaway: Shigella has a human reservoir and a very low infectious dose (about 10 organisms), so it spreads person to person (daycares) and causes invasive dysentery.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 30-year-old aid worker in a refugee camp after a flood develops sudden, painless, profuse watery diarrhea, many liters a day, that looks like cloudy water with no blood. He has no fever. Within hours he is lethargic with sunken eyes, tachycardia and low blood pressure, and labs show metabolic acidosis.

Which of the following is the mainstay of treatment?
choices: Antitoxin
Oral rehydration with salt, sugar and water
Intravenous ceftriaxone
An antimotility agent given alone to slow the stool output
Ampicillin

explain.html:
Massive, nonbloody watery diarrhea causing dehydration, acidosis and shock after drinking contaminated water is cholera, caused by Vibrio cholerae (serogroups O1 and O139 cause outbreaks). Its enterotoxin interferes with adenylate cyclase in mucosal cells, driving large-volume secretion without inflammation.

The bowel wall is not damaged, so it can still absorb salt and water when glucose is present. Oral rehydration solution (salt, sugar and water) is a very effective treatment and is the mainstay.
why: Antitoxin is used for botulism.
Ceftriaxone is used for typhoid fever.
Stopping motility does not replace the liters of fluid lost.
Ampicillin is used for invasive Listeria.
explain.takeaway: Cholera toxin acts on adenylate cyclase to cause massive secretory diarrhea, and oral rehydration with salt, sugar and water is the mainstay of treatment.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
On day 4 of a cruise, more than 200 passengers and crew develop vomiting, watery diarrhea, cramps, low-grade fever and myalgias, beginning 1 to 2 days after the first cases. Symptoms last 24 to 48 hours. New cases continue among people who ate different meals, even after the suspected buffet was closed. Bacterial stool cultures are negative.

Which of the following best explains why the outbreak continued after the food source was removed?
choices: Chronic carriers among the crew shed bacteria from the gallbladder
Spores germinated in food held at room temperature
A heat-stable toxin persisted in reheated food
Contaminated surfaces spread a highly infectious virus
Mosquitoes on board transmitted the virus

explain.html:
Explosive vomiting and diarrhea lasting 24 to 48 hours after a 12 to 72 hour incubation, with huge outbreaks on cruise ships and in hospitals, is norovirus, a calicivirus (formerly Norwalk-like virus). It probably causes the largest number of foodborne cases.

Norovirus is highly infectious, and surface contamination keeps it spreading person to person after the original food is gone. Molecular testing of stool can detect it.
why: Gallbladder carriage describes S. typhi.
Spore germination in held food explains B. cereus or C. perfringens, which do not keep spreading person to person.
A preformed toxin causes illness only in those who ate the food.
Norovirus is not mosquito-borne.
explain.takeaway: Norovirus (calicivirus, 12 to 72 hour incubation, 24 to 48 hour illness) is highly infectious and keeps spreading through contaminated surfaces in cruise ships and hospitals.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 15-year-old boy in northern Minnesota has 2 days of fever and severe right lower quadrant pain with tenderness. He has had little diarrhea. Two days before onset his family prepared pork intestines (chitterlings) for a holiday meal. At surgery the appendix is normal, but several mesenteric lymph nodes are markedly enlarged. Stool culture grows a gram-negative rod.

Which of the following organisms is most likely responsible?
choices: Bacillus cereus
Shigella sonnei
Vibrio cholerae
Enterotoxigenic E. coli
Yersinia enterocolitica

explain.html:
Fever and right lower quadrant pain that mimic appendicitis, with large mesenteric lymph nodes and a normal appendix, after eating pork intestines (chitterlings) in a cold climate, is Yersinia enterocolitica, a gram-negative rod.

Symptoms start 16 to 48 hours after ingestion. Diarrhea is more common in younger children and may be absent in older children and adults, which is why it can look like appendicitis. Diagnosis is by stool culture.
why: B. cereus causes vomiting or diarrhea from toxin, without fever and node enlargement.
Shigella causes dysentery with tenesmus and bloody stools, not pseudoappendicitis.
Cholera causes massive watery diarrhea without localized pain.
ETEC causes watery traveler's diarrhea.
explain.takeaway: Yersinia enterocolitica (cold climates, pork and chitterlings) causes fever with mesenteric adenitis that mimics appendicitis.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
Twenty minutes after eating grilled tuna that had been left unrefrigerated on a boat deck, a 40-year-old woman develops facial flushing, a burning sensation in her mouth and throat, headache, dizziness and mild cramps. Her companion, who ate the same fish, has similar symptoms. Neither has a history of fish allergy.

Which of the following best explains their symptoms?
choices: Histamine formed by bacteria acting on fish histidine
Dinoflagellate toxin accumulated in reef fish
Saxitoxin concentrated in bivalve mollusks
Preformed staphylococcal enterotoxin introduced into the fish by a handler
IgE-mediated allergy to fish protein

explain.html:
Flushing, mouth burning, headache and dizziness within minutes of eating poorly refrigerated fish, in more than one diner and without allergy, is scombroid (histamine fish poisoning). Marine bacteria in fish flesh convert histidine to histamine when the fish is not kept cold, producing a histamine reaction.

Other seafood toxins look different: ciguatera (dinoflagellate toxins) gives GI symptoms then numbness and paresthesias of the lips, tongue and throat, and saxitoxin from bivalve mollusks causes paralytic, neurotoxic or amnesic shellfish poisoning.
why: Ciguatera causes GI symptoms followed by perioral numbness and paresthesias.
Saxitoxin causes shellfish poisoning with paralysis or neurotoxicity.
Staph enterotoxin causes vomiting after hours, not flushing in minutes.
Two diners with no allergy history fit a toxin, not an individual allergy.
explain.takeaway: Scombroid is histamine fish poisoning from bacterial breakdown of histidine in poorly refrigerated fish, causing flushing, mouth burning and headache within minutes.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
Twelve guests at an outdoor July graduation party develop abrupt nausea, forceful vomiting and abdominal cramps about 3 hours after eating. None has fever. All are recovering by the next day. Every ill guest ate a potato salad made with mayonnaise and eggs that sat on a buffet table for several hours; the cook had a draining abscess on her finger. The leftover salad was thoroughly reheated before being tested.

Which property of the responsible agent explains why reheating did not make the leftover salad safe?
choices: Spores that germinate only after the food cools
A non-enveloped virus that resists drying on surfaces
An organism that multiplies at refrigerator temperatures
A toxin that resists heat once it has formed
Cysts that are resistant to chlorine in the water

explain.html:
Vomiting within a few hours of eating, no fever, resolution within 24 hours, a creamy egg and mayonnaise dish left at room temperature, and a food handler with a skin infection point to Staphylococcus aureus food poisoning. The short incubation means a preformed toxin was eaten, rather than bacteria that had to replicate in the gut.

S. aureus enterotoxins are heat stable and resist stomach acid and enzymes. Once the toxin has formed in the food, heating will not destroy it, even if it kills the bacteria. The diagnosis is confirmed by detecting toxin in the food.
why: Spore germination describes Bacillus cereus and Clostridium species, which are not linked to an infected food handler.
A hardy non-enveloped virus describes norovirus, with a 12 to 72 hour incubation.
Growth in the cold is a feature of Listeria.
Chlorine-resistant cysts or oocysts describe Cryptosporidium in water.
explain.takeaway: Staph aureus food poisoning causes vomiting 3 to 4 hours after a contaminated high-protein food; its preformed enterotoxin is heat stable, so reheating does not help.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 45-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with double vision, drooping eyelids, slurred speech and trouble swallowing that began about 24 hours after a dinner of home-canned green beans. Over several hours, weakness spreads to his arms and then his breathing becomes shallow. He is afebrile and fully alert, sensation is normal, and his mouth is dry. Pupils are dilated and poorly reactive.

Which of the following is the most important specific treatment?
choices: Ampicillin
Oral rehydration
Doxycycline
Antitoxin
Ceftriaxone

explain.html:
Cranial nerve palsies followed by a descending flaccid paralysis, with no fever, a clear sensorium, no sensory deficits and a dry mouth, 12 to 36 hours after eating home-canned food, is foodborne botulism. Clostridium botulinum spores germinate in low-oxygen canned food and produce an exotoxin that is absorbed from the gut and blocks neurotransmission at peripheral nerve synapses.

Treatment is antitoxin plus supportive care, including breathing support; recovery may take up to 100 days. Diagnosis is by toxin detection in blood, stool or vomit. Infant botulism follows honey, and wound botulism follows soil contamination of a wound.
why: Ampicillin is the treatment for invasive Listeria.
Oral rehydration is the mainstay for cholera, not a neuroparalytic toxin.
Doxycycline does not neutralize circulating botulinum toxin.
Ceftriaxone treats typhoid and gonorrhea, not botulism.
explain.takeaway: Foodborne botulism (home-canned food, afebrile descending flaccid paralysis with cranial nerve signs) is treated with antitoxin and supportive care.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 21-year-old college student develops abrupt watery, nonbloody diarrhea with cramps on the fourth day of a trip to Mexico, after eating salads and drinking tap-water ice. He has no fever. Stool shows no white blood cells. He improves in 3 days.

The main toxin of this organism acts most like which of the following?
choices: Shiga toxin, which halts protein synthesis in endothelium
Histamine formed in fish by marine bacteria
Botulinum toxin, which blocks acetylcholine release
Staphylococcal enterotoxin, which acts on central vomiting centers
Cholera toxin, which alters adenylate cyclase in enterocytes

explain.html:
Afebrile watery diarrhea without stool white cells in a traveler after uncooked food or contaminated water is traveler's diarrhea from enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC). Watery, large-volume diarrhea without white cells signals a secretory, toxin-mediated process rather than invasion.

ETEC makes a heat-labile toxin similar to cholera toxin, which alters adenylate cyclase in intestinal mucosal cells, and a heat-stable toxin; both increase fluid secretion. The illness is brief, and antibiotics are usually not needed (one dose, with or without an antimotility agent, is an option).
why: Shiga or verotoxin belongs to EHEC and Shigella, which cause bloody diarrhea.
Histamine causes scombroid flushing, not secretory diarrhea.
Botulinum toxin causes paralysis, not diarrhea.
Staphylococcal enterotoxin causes early vomiting, not traveler's diarrhea.
explain.takeaway: ETEC causes afebrile watery traveler's diarrhea through a heat-labile toxin that, like cholera toxin, alters adenylate cyclase and drives fluid secretion.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 6-year-old girl has 3 days of crampy abdominal pain and diarrhea that turned grossly bloody. She has no fever. Four days before onset she ate a hamburger at a county fair and petted calves. Stool culture identifies a sorbitol-negative E. coli, and an assay for a toxin in stool is positive.

Which of the following is the most appropriate management, and what complication should be watched for?
choices: Ciprofloxacin; watch for reactive arthritis
Azithromycin; watch for Guillain-Barre syndrome
Supportive care only; watch for hemolytic uremic syndrome
Ceftriaxone; watch for intestinal perforation
Oral metronidazole; watch for liver abscess

explain.html:
Bloody diarrhea without much fever in a child after undercooked beef and contact with cattle, with a positive stool toxin assay, is enterohemorrhagic E. coli, most often O157:H7. It produces verotoxin, almost identical to Shiga toxin; cattle and other livestock carry it in their gut.

EHEC can cause hemolytic uremic syndrome: thrombocytopenia, hemolytic anemia and renal failure that may be permanent, with children most severely affected. Antibiotics are not recommended; management is supportive.
why: Antibiotics are not recommended for EHEC, and reactive arthritis is linked to Campylobacter.
Guillain-Barre syndrome follows Campylobacter, and antibiotics are not used for EHEC.
Ceftriaxone and perforation risk belong to typhoid fever.
Metronidazole and liver abscess are not part of EHEC care.
explain.takeaway: EHEC O157:H7 (beef, cattle exposure) makes a Shiga-like verotoxin, causes bloody diarrhea and HUS, and is managed without antibiotics.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 9-year-old boy with sickle cell disease has 4 days of fever, bloody diarrhea and now severe pain in his left shin with point tenderness. His family recently bought a pet turtle. Stool culture on a selective medium grows a non-lactose-fermenting gram-negative rod, and blood cultures grow the same organism. Imaging of the tibia shows osteomyelitis.

Which of the following best explains why this patient developed bone infection?
choices: The organism makes a preformed toxin that travels to and injures bone directly
Infection was spread from the turtle by a tick
The organism forms spores that travel to bone
Sickle cell disease predisposes to invasive infection by this organism
Antibiotics given for the diarrhea caused bacteremia

explain.html:
A non-lactose-fermenting gram-negative rod causing febrile, sometimes bloody enterocolitis after reptile contact is Salmonella enteritidis. It invades through the terminal small intestine in the ileocecal region to the lamina propria, producing inflammation; reptiles and poultry are major reservoirs.

The usual illness is self-limited, but in patients with sickle cell disease, HIV or older age it can become invasive, causing septicemia, osteomyelitis and mycotic aneurysms. In uncomplicated GI illness antibiotics are usually not needed and can prolong carriage.
why: Salmonella invades the bowel; bone disease comes from bacteremia, not a preformed toxin.
Reptile Salmonella is acquired by handling the animal or its feces, not by ticks.
Salmonella is not a spore former.
Antibiotics do not cause bacteremia; they are given in high-risk hosts.
explain.takeaway: Salmonella enteritidis (poultry, eggs, reptiles) usually causes self-limited enterocolitis but invades in sickle cell disease, HIV and the elderly, causing sepsis and osteomyelitis.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
Public health investigators trace several cases of typhoid fever in a town to a 55-year-old woman who cooks for a catering company. She has never had a known febrile illness, but her stool cultures have grown Salmonella typhi repeatedly over the past 14 months. Ultrasound shows multiple gallstones.

Where is the organism most likely persisting?
choices: Gallbladder
Terminal ileum mucosa
Bone marrow
Mesenteric lymph nodes
Splenic red pulp

explain.html:
Chronic carriage of Salmonella typhi is defined by positive stool cultures for more than 12 months and occurs in 1 to 6% of infections, more often in women. Because S. typhi has no animal reservoir, human carriers sustain spread through food and water.

The gallbladder, especially with gallstones, is the classic reservoir; a urinary carrier state is linked to stones or schistosomiasis.
why: The terminal small intestine is where acute Salmonella infection invades, not the long-term carrier reservoir.
Bone marrow persistence is characteristic of Brucella.
Large mesenteric nodes mimicking appendicitis are a Yersinia enterocolitica feature.
The spleen is not the slide-listed site of chronic carriage.
explain.takeaway: Chronic S. typhi carriage (stool positive more than 12 months, more common in women) is usually in the gallbladder with gallstones.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 32-year-old man had 5 days of fever, cramps and bloody diarrhea after a backyard barbecue where he handled raw chicken. The stool laboratory needed a microaerophilic atmosphere and incubation at 42 C to grow a curved gram-negative rod. Three weeks after he recovered, he notices tingling in his feet, then symmetric weakness of his legs that climbs over several days, with absent ankle and knee reflexes.

Which of the following best describes his new illness?
choices: Reactivation of a latent virus residing in the dorsal root ganglia
Direct bacterial invasion of the spinal cord
A preformed toxin absorbed from undercooked chicken
A post-infectious complication of this enteric infection
A descending paralysis from an exotoxin

explain.html:
A curved gram-negative rod that needs microaerophilic, thermophilic (42 C) culture after contact with raw poultry is Campylobacter jejuni, one of the two most common causes of food-associated diarrhea in developed countries. Its diarrhea resembles Salmonella but can incubate and last longer.

Weeks later, an ascending symmetric weakness with areflexia is Guillain-Barre syndrome, a recognized post-infectious complication of Campylobacter, along with reactive arthritis. Severe Campylobacter diarrhea has been treated with erythromycin.
why: Latent virus in dorsal root ganglia describes herpesviruses, not this picture.
Campylobacter does not directly invade the spinal cord.
The weakness began weeks later and ascends, which does not fit a preformed toxin.
Descending paralysis from an exotoxin is botulism, which starts with cranial nerves.
explain.takeaway: Campylobacter jejuni (poultry; microaerophilic, grows at 42 C) causes bloody diarrhea and can be followed by Guillain-Barre syndrome or reactive arthritis.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 61-year-old man with alcoholic cirrhosis eats raw oysters at a Gulf Coast restaurant in August. Two days later he develops fever, then hypotension, and large fluid-filled blisters with purple discoloration on both legs. Blood pressure is 78/44 mm Hg. Blood cultures grow a curved gram-negative rod.

Which underlying condition most increases the risk of this severe presentation?
choices: Gallstones
Sickle cell disease with functional asplenia
Prior splenectomy
Pregnancy
Liver disease or iron overload

explain.html:
Septic shock with bullous skin lesions after eating raw oysters from warm coastal water is Vibrio vulnificus. Vibrio species can cause disease by ingestion or through wounds exposed to contaminated water, and are associated with shellfish, especially oysters.

In most people V. vulnificus causes diarrhea, but in patients with liver disease or iron storage disorders it causes severe systemic illness with fever, hypotension and bullae, and mortality exceeds 80%. Treatment is surgery and a tetracycline. Cases are moving north as coastal waters warm.
why: Gallstones are linked to chronic typhoid carriage.
Sickle cell disease predisposes to invasive Salmonella.
Splenectomy is the slide risk factor for severe babesiosis.
Pregnancy is a risk factor for invasive Listeria.
explain.takeaway: Vibrio vulnificus from raw oysters or seawater wounds causes sepsis with bullous skin lesions in patients with liver disease or iron overload, with mortality above 80%.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 29-year-old woman at 30 weeks of gestation has 2 days of fever, myalgias and back pain. She has eaten deli turkey and soft cheese from the refrigerator over the past month. Temperature is 38.9 C (102 F). Fetal heart tracing shows tachycardia. Blood cultures grow a motile gram-positive rod that grows well even at refrigerator temperatures.

Which of the following is the most appropriate antibiotic?
choices: Ceftriaxone
Erythromycin
Ampicillin
Ciprofloxacin
Metronidazole

explain.html:
A motile gram-positive rod that tolerates cold, acquired from deli meats and cheeses, causing bacteremia in a pregnant woman is Listeria monocytogenes. It causes illness in neonates, pregnant women, the elderly and immunocompromised patients, and invasive disease has a long incubation (average 30 days, up to 6 weeks).

In pregnancy it can cross the placenta and cause fetal death, premature birth or an infected baby; in adults it causes sepsis or meningitis. Diagnosis is by blood or CSF culture, and treatment is ampicillin.
why: Ceftriaxone is used for typhoid and is not the slide drug for Listeria.
Erythromycin is the slide option for severe Campylobacter diarrhea.
Ciprofloxacin is used for anthrax.
Metronidazole treats anaerobes and protozoa.
explain.takeaway: Listeria (cold-tolerant, deli meats and soft cheese) causes bacteremia in pregnancy that can infect the fetus; treat invasive disease with ampicillin.
explain.subject: Microbiology
